style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive prose) + amplified study form; em-dashes used sparingly; narrative register

1.text: Now Boaz went up to the gate and sat down there. And just then the kinsman-redeemer of whom Boaz had spoken came by. Boaz said, "Come over here, friend, and sit down." So he turned aside and sat down.
1.amp: ...the redeemer [go'el] of whom Boaz had spoken passed by; he said, 'Turn aside, friend [peloni almoni -- literally 'so-and-so,' the man left deliberately unnamed], sit here.'
1.notes: The town gate was the courtroom and council chamber of Israel. The narrator pointedly leaves the nearer redeemer unnamed ('such a one') -- the man who would not raise up the dead man's name forfeits his own in the record, while Boaz's name endures.

2.text: Then Boaz took ten men of the elders of the town and said, "Sit down here." And they sat down.
2.notes: Ten elders form the legal quorum and witnesses -- Boaz does everything openly, lawfully, and before the whole community.

3.text: And he said to the kinsman-redeemer, "Naomi, who has come back from the country of Moab, is selling the parcel of land that belonged to our brother Elimelech.
3.notes: Boaz opens with the land, the redeemer's first concern. The duty of the go'el included buying back family land that poverty had forced onto the market (Lev. 25:25), keeping the inheritance in the family.

4.text: So I thought I would bring it to your attention and say: buy it back in the presence of those sitting here and of the elders of my people. If you will redeem it, redeem it; but if you will not, tell me, so I may know — for there is no one to redeem it but you, and I am after you." And he said, "I will redeem it."
4.notes: The nearer kinsman gladly accepts the land alone -- it enlarges his estate at little cost. He does not yet know the condition attached.

5.text: Then Boaz said, "On the day you buy the field from the hand of Naomi, you also acquire Ruth the Moabitess, the widow of the dead, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance."
5.amp: ...to raise up the name of the dead [yibbum -- the levirate duty: marrying the widow so her firstborn carries the dead husband's name and inheritance] upon his inheritance.
5.notes: The redeemer's duty was not land only but the widow with it (Deut. 25:5-6). The first son born would legally be Mahlon's heir, not the redeemer's -- inheriting the very land just purchased. The cost suddenly outweighs the gain.

6.text: At that the kinsman-redeemer said, "Then I cannot redeem it for myself, or I would ruin my own inheritance. Take my right of redemption yourself, for I cannot redeem it."
6.amp: ...lest I ruin [shachat -- mar/destroy] my own inheritance; you redeem it yourself.
6.notes: shachat (H7843) = to spoil/ruin. The nearer kinsman counts the cost and withdraws -- unwilling to spend himself on another man's name. His self-protection clears the way for Boaz, who will spend himself freely. The contrast frames the gospel shape of redemption: the redeemer must be willing to lose for the sake of another.

7.text: Now this was the custom in earlier times in Israel concerning redemption and exchange: to confirm a matter, a man would take off his sandal and give it to the other; this was the manner of attesting in Israel.
7.notes: Removing and handing over the sandal publicly transferred a right (cf. Deut. 25:9; Ps. 60:8) -- the ancient equivalent of a signature and seal before witnesses.

8.text: So the kinsman-redeemer said to Boaz, "Buy it for yourself," and he drew off his sandal.
8.notes: With the sandal, the nearer kinsman's right passes to Boaz before all the witnesses -- the transaction is sealed and legal.

9.text: Boaz then declared to the elders and to all the people, "This day you stand as witnesses: from Naomi's hand I have purchased everything that was Elimelech's, together with all that belonged to Chilion and to Mahlon.
9.notes: Boaz buys back everything the family had lost -- redeeming the inheritance whole, openly, and at his own cost.

10.text: And I have also acquired Ruth the Moabitess, the widow of Mahlon, to be my wife, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance, so that the name of the dead may not be cut off from among his brothers and from the gate of his town. You are witnesses today."
10.notes: Boaz takes the widow and her dead husband's name as his glad purpose, not his burden. The foreign widow is brought fully into Israel and the covenant -- redeemed, named, and secured.

11.text: Then all the people at the gate, and the elders, said, "We are witnesses. May the LORD make the woman coming into your house like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel. May you prosper in Ephrathah and be renowned in Bethlehem.
11.amp: ...like Rachel and Leah, who both built [banah -- built up, the root behind 'house' and 'son'] the house of Israel.
11.notes: banah (H1129) = to build (of a family/household). The town blesses the Moabitess as a mother of Israel, ranked with the matriarchs -- the outsider grafted in. 'Be renowned' is literally 'proclaim a name,' fitting for a story all about raising up a name.

12.text: And may your house be like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah, through the offspring the LORD will give you by this young woman."
12.notes: Perez too was born of a redeemer-marriage to a once-foreign widow (Tamar, Gen. 38). The blessing reaches back into Judah's line -- and forward, for Perez stands at the head of the genealogy that ends in David (vv.18-22).

13.text: So Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife. And he went in to her, and the LORD enabled her to conceive, and she bore a son.
13.amp: ...and the LORD gave her conception [the one explicit act of God in the book -- the womb opened by His direct gift].
13.notes: The whole book has shown the LORD's hidden hand in 'chance' and kindness; here at the climax His work is named outright. The barrenness and death of chapter 1 give way to life He Himself grants.

14.text: Then the women said to Naomi, "Blessed be the LORD, who today has not let you go without a kinsman-redeemer! May his name be celebrated in Israel.
14.amp: ...who has not left you without a redeemer [go'el] today.
14.notes: The women bless the LORD for the go'el. Strikingly, the redeemer they celebrate is finally the newborn child -- the line preserved -- as much as Boaz. The book that opened with three funerals closes with a birth and a blessing.

15.text: He will be to you a restorer of life and a sustainer of your old age; for your daughter-in-law, who loves you and is better to you than seven sons, has given him birth."
15.amp: He will be a restorer of life [meshib nephesh -- one who brings your very soul back] and a sustainer of your old age, for your daughter-in-law who loves you, who is better to you than seven sons [the proverbial perfect number of heirs], has borne him.
15.notes: meshib nephesh (H7725/H5315) = 'one who returns the soul' -- the same phrase as 'He restores my soul' in Psalm 23:3. Naomi, who said she came home 'empty,' is now called full -- and Ruth the Moabitess is honored above seven sons. The emptiness of 1:21 is wholly reversed.

16.text: And Naomi took the child, laid him on her lap, and became his nurse.
16.notes: The grandmother who called herself 'Mara, bitter' now cradles new life on her lap -- grief swallowed up in the LORD's quiet mercy.

17.text: And the women, her neighbors, gave him a name, saying, "A son has been born to Naomi." They named him Obed; he is the father of Jesse, the father of David.
17.notes: Obed (H5744) = 'servant/worshiper.' The local, tender story suddenly opens onto the whole sweep of redemption: this child is grandfather to David -- and so the Moabite widow's loyal love is woven into the royal line that leads, in time, to the Son of David, the true Kinsman-Redeemer (Matt. 1:5).

18.text: Now these are the generations of Perez: Perez was the father of Hezron,
18.notes: The closing genealogy (vv.18-22) runs ten names from Perez to David, anchoring this household tale in the grand line of promise.

19.text: Hezron's son was Ram, and Ram's son Amminadab,

20.text: Amminadab's son was Nahshon, and Nahshon's son Salmon,

21.text: Salmon's son was Boaz, and Boaz's son Obed,

22.text: and Obed's son was Jesse, and Jesse's son was David.
22.notes: The book ends on the name it has been quietly building toward: David. A famine, two funerals, a foreign widow's hesed, and a redeemer's costly love -- all of it, unseen, was the LORD weaving the line of the king, and beyond him the King.
